| `distribution_shift` | exact empirical-CDF Wasserstein $W_1$ and two-sample KS $D$; stable asymptotic KS $p$ | sort plus linear CDF merge, including ties and unequal sizes; $D=0$ → $p=1$; both halves need $\ge2$ observations; $p$ is not calibrated for tied/fitted distributions |
| `trending_features` | feature names with Mann–Kendall $p < 0.05$ | summary list |
| `segmented_features` | feature names with at least one guarded-objective changepoint | summary list |
| `shifted_features` | feature names with early/late KS $p < 0.05$ | summary list |
| `cooccurrence` *(token-level)* | content-word graph (window 2; single-character tokens excluded); approximate discrete exponent $\hat\alpha=1+n/\sum\ln(k_i/(k_{\min}-0.5))$ and fitted-CDF comparison | estimator follows Clauset–Shalizi–Newman Eq. 3.7; current truncated continuous CDF and ordinary KS $p$ do not establish discrete power-law goodness of fit; ≥50 content tokens, ≥5 positive nonconstant degrees |
| `keyness` *(token-level)* | **Dunning $G^2$** (log-likelihood ratio) of first-half chapters vs second half, content words only (single-character tokens excluded); signed so positive = over in the early half | both halves ≥ 20 content tokens; single-chapter texts omit `keyness` |

The legacy Python name `pelt_changepoints` is retained, but the implementation
does not prune or claim linear time. Its guarded singleton/constant cost does
not satisfy the PELT pruning premise in
[Killick et al., Theorem 3.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.1438v3). Considering
every predecessor corrects optimization of this declared objective; the guard
is still a modelling choice, not a nondegenerate Gaussian likelihood. Anchoring
before centred variance updates limits cancellation from large offsets without
recovering precision already lost in input floats.

Sn's low/high medians follow the
[original definition](https://wis.kuleuven.be/stat/robust/papers/publications-1993/rousseeuwcroux-alternativestomedianad-jasa-1993.pdf).
Qn uses the modern rounded Gaussian factor 2.21914 instead of historical
2.2219, preserving its order-statistic rank. These normalizations remain
separate from finite-sample bias correction; neither estimator applies it.

Wasserstein distance integrates $|F_{\mathrm{early}}-F_{\mathrm{late}}|$ over
the distinct empirical-CDF knots. KS $D$ is the maximum CDF difference on the
same merged support. Stable evaluation of the asymptotic survival function
corrects the identical-distribution boundary and small-argument cancellation;
it does not turn the approximate $p$ into an exact, fitted-null or tied-data
calibration. Short samples and serially dependent chapters need care.

Token-level blocks (`cooccurrence`, `keyness`) are computed by
`lexical_structural_diagnostics(text, config)` and merged into
`structural_diagnostics` on the text-bearing surfaces (`api.fingerprint`,
CLI `style` / `build` / `dashboard`). `StyleFingerprint.from_metrics`
alone still yields the metric-derived keys only.

Keyness uses the full term/non-term × corpus A/B contingency table. Expected
counts are row-total × column-total / grand-total, and
$G^2 = 2\sum O\ln(O/E)$, with zero observed cells contributing zero. Lixity adds
a direction sign for over-representation in A. This follows the binomial
likelihood-ratio formulation in [Dunning (1993), §5.3](https://aclanthology.org/J93-1003.pdf).
Version 1.16.0 includes the non-term cells previously omitted from this calculation;
recompute older keyness values before comparison. A signed ranking is not a
multiple-testing-adjusted significance claim.

The passport retains schema 4 and these field names. The structural summary
uses the implemented thresholds; it does not certify a narrative boundary,
trend or fitted distribution. See [STABILITY.md](STABILITY.md#structural-diagnostics)
for the model assumptions and current calculation limits.

### Track B / research extensions (not implemented)

Documented research directions, **not** current product features:

- **Textometry / Burrows’ Delta** (and 2026 generalisations to Jensen–
  Shannon / Rank-Turbulence Delta): authorship-attribution baselines.
  Lixity’s chapter↔rest JSD with driver words is *inspired by* this line
  but deliberately **not** an attribution instrument (see STABILITY §1).
  There is **no external Delta stylometry** against a reference corpus;
  a future Delta panel would rank chapters against such a corpus — out of
  scope while the product stays manuscript-intrinsic. Structure-module
  caveats (empty `signal_counts`, filter-list definitions, pacing without
  dividers, no NER/speaker attribution) are registered in STABILITY §2
  and summarised in AGENTS §3.5.
- **OHCO / TEI**: OHCO means [Ordered Hierarchy of Content Objects](https://experts.illinois.edu/en/publications/what-is-text-really/),
  a document-model thesis; TEI supplies scholarly text-encoding guidelines. Lixity’s input contract
  is UTF-8 Markdown with `## ` chapter headings (configurable
  `chapter_regex` / `appendix_marker`); a TEI→Markdown ingest path would be
  the natural bridge, not a second analysis core.
- **Hermeneutic loop / Foregrounding (Mukařovský)**: deviation from a
  text’s *own* norm is the literary signal — already the design principle
  of the self-calibrating house style. A deeper hermeneutic layer (quotes,
  interpretive commentary tied to flagged cells) is UI/agent territory, not
  a new estimator.

### Track C / pedagogy (not implemented)

- Worked examples that walk one chapter from KPI → heatmap → paragraph →
  marker, suitable as a tutorial on the project page.
- Glossary of every passport key for non-statisticians (beyond `llms.txt`).
- Exportable “method card” (estimator + citation + guard) per metric for
  peer review / replication packages.

## 5. Exploratory style dimensions

The dimensions are PCA of standardized tied midranks on one common complete
chapter set. Covariance, loadings, explained variance and scores use that same
rank space:

1. Start with baseline-usable features and select chapters measured on every
   candidate feature. At least three complete chapters are required.
2. Give tied values their average rank within this set. Centre each rank column
   and divide by its sample standard deviation ($n-1$ denominator). Drop
   columns constant on this set; at least three varying features must remain.
3. Form $C=X^\mathsf{T}X/(n-1)$ and use cyclic Jacobi eigendecomposition
   (standard library only). Eigenvalues are sorted descending; the
   largest-absolute loading fixes each axis sign.
4. Project the same standardized ranks: $s_k=Xv_k$. Only the common complete
   chapters receive `scores`; missing measurements are not imputed. The
   reported `variance` is $\lambda_k/p$ for $p$ unit-variance columns, the
   explained fraction in this rank space.
5. A completed, unrounded score with |score| ≥ `dim_score_threshold` (default
   2.5) puts a chapter in `flagged` on that axis. Scores are stored rounded to
   two decimals; the cutoff remains descriptive, not a calibrated probability.

Fewer than three complete chapters or varying features yields no dimensions.
Incomplete chapters remain available in the other measured-feature views but
do not receive dimension scores. The complete-case subset can be small or
unrepresentative, and ranks depend on the supplied manuscript. Explained
variance does not mean literary importance or a simultaneous confidence region.

The separate redundancy list still compares each pair's available chapters:
|Spearman $\rho$| ≥ `REDUNDANCY_RHO` (0.8). Pairwise availability in that list
does not define the PCA matrix or its scoring population. The list is capped
at the ten strongest pairs.

## 6. Lexical diversity indices

| Index | Definition sketch | Guard |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Guiraud $R$ | $\mathrm{TTR} \sqrt{N}$ | length-dependent; prefer with HD-D |
| HD-D | hypergeometric expected TTR of one 42-token draw without replacement from whole-text type frequencies | $\ge 100$ tokens else `null` |
| MTLD | arithmetic mean $\tfrac12(N/F_{\mathrm{forward}}+N/F_{\mathrm{reverse}})$; factor completes at TTR ≤0.72; trailing weight $(1-\mathrm{TTR})/(1-0.72)$ | $\ge100$ tokens; zero factors/all-unique input → `null`; no minimum run length |
| MATTR | mean TTR over sliding 50-token windows | window length |
| Maas $a^2$ | $a^2 = (\log_{10} N - \log_{10} V)/(\log_{10} N)^2$ | $\ge 100$ tokens; base 10 as in the implementation |
| Yule $K$ | $10^4 \cdot (\sum m^2 V_m - N)/N^2$ | length-dependent by design |

MTLD now averages directional $N/F$ scores arithmetically, following the
original-style `mtldo` aggregation in the
[author-lab TAALED reference](https://github.com/LCR-ADS-Lab/TAALED/blob/f3c39692b01efa84e39e4de69f8ac109ac1c4bcd/taaled/ld.py).
The previous combination averaged factors first, yielding the harmonic mean
of directional scores. Lixity retains its inclusive threshold, fractional
remainder, no minimum run length and local availability policies. TAALED's
segmentation conventions differ, so complete tool equivalence is not claimed.
The original McCarthy–Jarvis full paper was unavailable for this review; the
author-lab source supports the narrower aggregation claim. See
[STABILITY.md](STABILITY.md#lexical-diversity) for comparison limits.

The 100-token floor is a local short-text policy, not a universal reliability
threshold. Maas is defined for a one-type text: $N=100$, $V=1$ gives $a^2=0.5$.
Only a nonpositive type count or an input below the token floor is unavailable;
repetition alone is not a missing measurement. Guiraud $R=V/\sqrt{N}$ remains
length-dependent and does not make arbitrary texts directly comparable.

For $N$ tokens, type counts $f_t$, and draw size $d=42$, the implemented
expectation is

$$
\mathrm{HD\text{-}D} = \frac{1}{d}\sum_t
\left(1-\frac{\binom{N-f_t}{d}}{\binom{N}{d}}\right),
$$

where $\binom{N-f_t}{d}=0$ if fewer than $d$ non-$t$ tokens remain. The
frequency histogram makes the result independent of token order. The public
`seed` and `min_samples` arguments remain accepted legacy no-ops that emit a
`DeprecationWarning` when explicitly supplied. Ordinary calls omit them and
remain warning-free. The second value of `hd_d_stats` is `0.0` because this
exact expectation has no Monte Carlo sampling error; it does not estimate
uncertainty about a population of possible texts.

Before version 1.16.0, the `hd_d` key held mean Gini–Simpson diversity over
sampled, contiguous 35-token windows, with a window-based plug-in SE. Those
numbers are **not comparable** with corrected HD-D even though the JSON key is
unchanged. Reanalyze the original manuscript and regenerate chapter metrics,
style baselines, reports, and passports before comparing or publishing results
across that boundary. The new 100-token floor also makes values available for
100–174-token inputs that previously returned `null` by default.

## 7. Language-specific readability

Seven named formula variants, selected by profile; the implemented coefficients
are fixed and covered by hand-computed tests:

| Lang | Formula (name) | Implemented formula |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| de | Amstad / Flesch-De | $180 - 1.0\cdot\mathrm{ASL} - 58.5\cdot\mathrm{ASW}$ |
| en | Flesch | $206.835 - 1.015\cdot\mathrm{ASL} - 84.6\cdot\mathrm{ASW}$ |
| fr | Kandel-Moles | $207.0 - 1.015\cdot\mathrm{ASL} - 73.6\cdot\mathrm{ASW}$ |
| es | Szigriszt-Pazos | $206.835 - 1.0\cdot\mathrm{ASL} - 62.35\cdot\mathrm{ASW}$ |
| it | Franchina-Vacca | $217.0 - 1.3\cdot\mathrm{ASL} - 60.0\cdot\mathrm{ASW}$ |
| pt | Martins | $248.835 - 1.015\cdot\mathrm{ASL} - 84.6\cdot\mathrm{ASW}$ |
| nl | Douma | $207.0 - 0.93\cdot\mathrm{ASL} - 77.0\cdot\mathrm{ASW}$ |

$\mathrm{ASL}$ = words per sentence; $\mathrm{ASW}$ = syllables per word
(heuristic syllable counter), not syllables per 100 words. These scores are
not clipped to 0–100. Empty or fully unmeasurable input returns `0.0` as an
explicit unavailable sentinel, not a readability score. The coefficients above match `language_data.READABILITY`;
correct formula dispatch is not empirical validation on every manuscript. **LIX** uses the
standard Björnsson cut: words with **more than six characters**, for every
language: $\mathrm{LIX} = \mathrm{ASL} + 100 \cdot \frac{\text{long words}}{\text{tokens}}$.

The Spanish syllable estimate counts orthographic vowel nuclei: standalone
closed vowels (`i`, `u`) count, open/unstressed-closed combinations and distinct
closed-vowel pairs can share a nucleus, and marked hiatus remains separate.
Triphthongs use the closed/open/closed pattern. Standard silent `u` in
`que`/`qui`/`gue`/`gui` is omitted; pronounced `ü` is retained, and interposed
`h` does not itself block grouping. These bounded spelling rules follow the
RAE/ASALE explanations of [diphthongs](https://www.rae.es/dpd/diptongo),
[hiatus](https://www.rae.es/dpd/hiato) and [the letter u](https://www.rae.es/dpd/u).
They are an orthographic proxy, not phonetic transcription: regional hiatus,
foreign names and loans, and poetic synaeresis remain outside the estimate.
Regression examples do not establish language-wide accuracy or reader comprehension.

**Since v0.7.2:** the estimator corrects skipped closed-vowel nuclei in Spanish, for example
`vivir` from one estimated syllable to two and `dibujo` from one to three.
This changes Spanish ASW and its derived readability score without changing
the formula coefficients or JSON fields. Regenerate Spanish reports before
comparing results across this correction.

## 8. Jensen–Shannon divergence (chapter ↔ rest)

$JSD(P \| Q) = \tfrac12 D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \| M) + \tfrac12 D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q \| M)$
with $M = \tfrac12(P+Q)$. The implementation uses natural logarithms, so the
divergence is in $[0,\ln 2]$ nats. It is zero for identical distributions,
regardless of their token counts. This is the equal-weight form of
[Lin's Jensen–Shannon divergence (1991, §IV)](https://www.cise.ufl.edu/~anand/sp06/jensen-shannon.pdf).
Driver words present in the chapter are ranked by their positive additive
contribution, excluding function words and single-character tokens.
Types absent from the chapter contribute half their rest-corpus probability
times $\ln 2$; their total probability is calculated from the observed rest
distribution. No square root or base-2 rescaling is applied.

**Since v0.7.2:** absent-type mass is computed from remaining
integer token counts, and contributions are accumulated with `math.fsum`.
Near equal probabilities, the same per-type contribution is evaluated as
$m[d\mathrm{atanh}(d)+\tfrac12\ln(1-d^2)]$, where
$m=(p+q)/2$ and $d=(p-q)/(p+q)$; the contrast is derived from count cross-products
before probabilities are rounded. This avoids cancellation of first-order
logarithmic terms. No fixed epsilon suppresses small genuine divergence.
Unchanged-rate words are omitted from the driver list; identical distributions
return zero and an empty list. The definition, natural-log units and JSON fields
are unchanged.

Version 1.16.0 corrects the absent-type probability calculation, which could
previously produce negative divergence. Recompute older metrics before comparing
chapter profiles across this release. With no chapter tokens or no remaining
corpus tokens, `0.0` and an empty driver list mean unavailable, rather than
measured agreement. JSD uses empirical token frequencies and ignores word order
and narrative context. Its values and driver rankings are descriptive; they
provide no calibrated probability, significance test, quality assessment,
attribution or historical-accuracy judgment.

## 9. Paragraph layers (within-chapter colouring)

Each chapter is its own reference: robust $z$ of the paragraph value against
that chapter’s paragraph median/MAD ($n \ge 3$ measurable paragraphs, else
skipped). Layer fill uses the absolute value span (min–max per dimension);
the ring marks $\lvert z \rvert \ge 1.5$ (unusual **for this chapter**).

The separate showing/telling composite standardizes each raw signal against
the manuscript's chapter median/MAD, then averages each group with equal
feature weights (four telling and two showing signals); zero spread uses the
population standard deviation when available.
Fewer than three chapters or zero spread produce zero component scores.
`most_telling` and `most_showing` are empty when all balances are identical,
including this insufficient-data fallback; chapter-order ties are not evidence
of a ranking. These signals describe relative patterns, not prose quality.

## 10. Determinism contract

- No wall-clock in the analysis path; HD-D is an exact frequency calculation.
- Float operations in fixed order on the same interpreter → byte-identical
  HTML/JSON (platform last-bit differences are documented in STABILITY).

## 11. Linguistic heuristics (tense, dialogue, sentences, scenes)

These heuristics are transparent rules over curated resources, not a
grammatical parser. Their constants and guards live in the named modules.
Shared mathematical primitives (robust scale, significance z, normal tail,
ratio/share/density totalization, plug-in standard errors and published effect
bands) come from `lixity.math_core`; heuristics import them instead of
restating formulas.

| Heuristic | Rule | Limits |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Sentence bins | ≤ 6 / 7–15 / 16–25 / > 25 words (`analyzer.py`, `pacing.py`) | Bins describe the supplied text; tokenless fragments distort ASL |
| Hook | First sentence ≤ `HOOK_SHORT_SENTENCE` (8) words or ending in `…` (`pacing.py`) | Only the ellipsis character scores; `...` does not |
| Dialogue paragraph | ≥ 50 % of the paragraph's words inside dialogue spans (`dialogue.py`) | Quotation conventions differ per language |
| Tense mixed/switch | `mixed`: ≥ 2 present and ≥ 2 past markers and minority share ≥ 25 %; `switch`: the dominant tense changes between consecutive paragraphs (`style_profile.py`) | Whole-word stop lists and curated noun exclusions; German `-tet` intentionally omitted (present `arbeitet`, participle `abgewartet` vs rare past 2pl `machtet`); no productive present pattern |
| Sentence splitter | Language abbreviation tables, digit and initial guards; utterance `no.`/`co.` split; prose splits keep blank-line block boundaries (`split_prose_sentences`) | Tables are curated and incomplete; tokenless fragments are not sentences; an unterminated block stays one fragment unit with its token length |
| Severity | `classify_severity` truth table; defaults: 3 = switch + mixed + minority ≥ 3, 2 = (switch + minority ≥ 2) or (mixed + minority ≥ 3), 1 = either, 0 = neither | Only `flag_min_severity` reaches CLI/API/config; other `ProfileThresholds` fields need direct `ParagraphProfiler` construction |
| Dominance | past when `past/(present+ε) > 1.5`, present when `< 0.67` (`style_profile.py`) | Ratio bands are conventions, not measured boundaries |
| Nominal/adjective suffixes | Curated suffix cues minus curated function words (`language_data.py`) | Over-include (e.g. `month/health/truth`, `König/Saal`, `Musik/Natur`) |
| Modal lexicons | Curated forms per language | Unequal morphology coverage; not cross-language comparable |

Configured cue patterns override the profile patterns for direct Python calls.
Cue patterns (including `dialogue_regex`) use the case-insensitive cue
contract from §2 across the analysis core and the `dialogue`/`pacing` reports.
- `python -W error` test run + `mypy --strict` + ruff gate every change.

## Where to plug new thresholds

| Surface | Hook |
| :--- | :--- |
| CLI | `--z-mild`, `--z-strong`, `--fdr-q`, `--fdr-method`, `--dim-threshold`, `--flag-min-severity` (see USAGE) |
| API | `api.fingerprint(..., z_mild=…, fdr_q=…, fdr_method=…, …)` |
| Control UI | Settings group → POST `/api/settings` → `lixity.server.LixityServerHandler` |
| Embedders | `build_dashboard_html(..., z_mild=…, z_strong=…, fdr_q=…, flag_min_severity=…, dim_score_threshold=…)` |
| Config file | `[tool.lixity]` in `pyproject.toml`, or `lixity.toml` / `~/.config/lixity.toml` |
| Tests | `FingerprintThresholds(...)` + passport `meta` |

Resolution order per key: CLI/API flag → UI session → project config →
user config → code default (`src/lixity/config.py`).

## Method currency and recent literature

The lexical-diversity and readability choices follow the current methodological
literature and are re-checked when it changes:

- **Length dependence.** Bestgen's 2024 methodological review confirms that the
  classic length problem of lexical diversity is addressed by length-reducing
  indices, but that the reduction parameter itself becomes a source of
  variance. The review recommends HD-D for an overall score and MATTR/MTLD for
  local trajectories, with a fixed parameter for cross-text comparability.
  Lixity computes HD-D on a 42-token draw — the review's preferred value for
  comparability — reports MTLD and MATTR with fixed windows, and treats
  per-chapter values as short-text estimates. The same review shows that MATTR
  weights tokens by position, which is why Lixity reports it as a local measure
  and keeps HD-D as the corpus-level index.
- **Minimum text lengths.** Koizumi & In'nami (2012) and Zenker & Kyle (2020)
  quantify when lexical-diversity indices stabilise. Lixity states these limits
  in the interface and marks unavailable results instead of hiding them.
- **Measurement noise.** Kyle et al. (2024) evaluate reliability and validity of
  lexical-diversity indices against proficiency scores. Lixity follows the same
  principle with its standard-error approximations (`style_se`) and the
  noise-adjusted deviation `z*` rather than presenting a bare rank.

Adjacent tasks are deliberately out of scope. Authorship attribution and
LLM-generated-text detection are separate research fields with their own
benchmarks and models (Huang et al. 2024; Weerasinghe et al. 2025); their
results depend on the candidate set, the domain and the generator version.
Lixity describes the observable patterns of one manuscript. Every signal stays a
prompt for reading, never a verdict about authorship, quality or machine origin.

References:

- Bestgen, Y. (2024). *The impact of text length on the estimation of lexical
  diversity: A methodological review.* (Length problem, HD-D/MATTR/MTLD
  recommendations, parameter 42.)
- Bestgen, Y. (2024). *Estimating lexical diversity using the moving average
  type-token ratio (MATTR): Pros and cons.* (Positional weighting of MATTR.)
- Covington, M. A., & McFall, J. D. (2010). Cutting the Gordian knot: The
  moving-average type-token ratio (MATTR). *Journal of Quantitative
  Linguistics* 17(2), 94–100. doi:10.1080/09296171003643098
- Huang, R., et al. (2024). *Authorship attribution in the era of LLMs:
  Problems, methodologies, and challenges.* arXiv:2408.08946.
- Koizumi, R., & In'nami, Y. (2012). Effects of text length on lexical
  diversity measures. *System* 40(4), 554–564. doi:10.1016/j.system.2012.10.012
- Kyle, K., Sung, H., Eguchi, M., & Zenker, F. (2024). Evaluating evidence for
  the reliability and validity of lexical diversity indices. *Studies in Second
  Language Acquisition* 46(1), 278–299. doi:10.1017/S0272263123000402
- McCarthy, P. M., & Jarvis, S. (2010). MTLD, vocd-D, and HD-D: A validation
  study. *Behavior Research Methods* 42(2), 381–392. doi:10.3758/BRM.42.2.381
- Weerasinghe, J., et al. (2025). Be sure to use the same writing style:
  Applying authorship verification on large-language-model-generated texts.
  *Applied Sciences* 15(5), 2467. doi:10.3390/app15052467
- Zenker, F., & Kyle, K. (2020). Investigating minimum text lengths for lexical
  diversity indices. *Assessing Writing* 47, 100505.
  doi:10.1016/j.asw.2020.100505

## docs/STABILITY.md

Source: https://github.com/mfahsold/lixity/blob/main/docs/STABILITY.md

# Stability & known limitations

Use this page to judge what a result can support. Formula details live in
[METHODS.md](METHODS.md); machine-readable thresholds and availability policies
come from `lixity about --json`. This page keeps interpretation and integration
limits that a passing check cannot resolve. Statistical signals support human
review, not a prose grade.

## 1. Research findings (state of the art)

### Release verification and limits

The maintained suite checks English defaults, language resource-key coverage,
readability-coefficient dispatch and locale formatting. These are software
contracts, not empirical validation of linguistic accuracy across seven
languages. No language-wide accuracy percentage is established by this suite.

The 3D chapter view is exploratory: its dimensions are corpus-specific, signs
are fixed by convention, and per-axis thresholds are not simultaneous confidence
regions. Native rotation/zoom buttons and a chapter-score table provide keyboard and touch access to the displayed scores,
flag status and chapter navigation. Individual canvas points remain pointer-operated.
These targeted checks do not establish full assistive-technology coverage.

Engine tests use synthetic/public samples. Project adapters and optional local
servers have separate trust boundaries and need their own tests; core test
success is not a security certification for an arbitrary adapter.

### Manual manuscript association limits

Manually selected quotes require explicit retention and exact source/paragraph/claim
pins. Anchor review detects structural changes, not semantic contradictions or
factual support. Moved or ambiguous quotes require review; claim pins change only
through an explicit revision. Zero saved links do not prove a claim is unused.
The source recheck is optimistic and does not lock manuscript editors. Backups
include retained private quotes; this workflow creates no full manuscript blob.
See [retention and compatibility](research/USAGE.md#associate-a-manuscript-quote-with-a-claim).

### Research and external-library limits

Zotero owns bibliography and reading; Lixity retains selected evidence and authored
records. Their backup requirements are separate. An integrity audit verifies
retained bytes, references and citations; it cannot verify historical truth,
chronology or the completeness of an external library. Native integration checks
are bounded synthetic tests, not certification of every platform or collection.

Source analysis uses its own `source_internal` reference and unverified supplied
context. Retaining a historical source does not make it a manuscript style norm;
lexical overlap does not establish factual support or appropriate context.
Search does not resolve contradictory prose or accept a hypothesis for the author.

PNG/JPEG images retain exact source versions and stay outside text analysis.
Header validation and browser preview do not establish complete codec validity or
historical authenticity. Geographic coordinates and routes are authored data;
rendering a map does not verify a journey or sightline. An unavailable image
never silently resolves to a different version.

RIS migration is additive; verify attachment identities, retained citations and
restoration before retiring a workflow. Automatic background/cloud synchronization,
audio/video transcription, image OCR and visual AI are not implemented. PDF
extraction or an external OCR worker does not establish recognition accuracy.
Current media, provider and schema boundaries live in [Research usage](research/USAGE.md).

### Robust comparisons and statistical claims

Median/MAD and the noise-adjusted $z^*$ describe contrast within the supplied
manuscript. A normal-consistency multiplier does not make arbitrary chapter
features normally distributed. Missing SE means no estimated measurement error;
zero event counts or constant samples do not establish certainty.

BH/BY are established selection procedures **given valid null probabilities**
and their dependence conditions. Lixity's normal-tail probabilities use a
baseline estimated from the same chapters; their calibration is not established.
BY, runs/lag diagnostics and the `low_power` flag do not repair that gap.
`fdr_flagged` means selected under the implemented model, and
`expected_false_positives` is a standard-normal reference expectation, not an
observed error count. Cliff's delta describes ordinal contrast, not quality.
Definitions and active thresholds: [METHODS §§1–4](METHODS.md#1-robust-house-style-baseline).

Style axes now use PCA of standardized tied midranks on one common complete
chapter set. Covariance, explained variance and scores share that rank space;
missing measurements are not imputed. At least three complete chapters and
three varying baseline-usable features are required, with constant columns
dropped on that set. Incomplete chapters have no dimension scores. Complete-case selection and small samples still limit interpretation. Score flags are
descriptive and do not validate prose quality or simultaneous confidence.
See [METHODS §5](METHODS.md#5-exploratory-style-dimensions).

### Lexical diversity

Length, local vocabulary and estimator parameters affect different indices.
[Bestgen (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12630) studies English learner essays
and monologues; 60 tokens is one truncation condition, not a universal floor.
Its main experiment uses a 50-token draw/window parameter, so it does not
directly calibrate Lixity's 42-token HD-D.
[Kyle et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263123000402) assesses optimized
oral-task variants, not Lixity's defaults on German novels. Neither establishes
genre-wide reliability for the local 100-token policy. Guiraud remains sensitive
to length; fixed-window MATTR and fixed-draw HD-D still depend on their parameters
and the supplied vocabulary distribution.

HD-D is exact expected TTR for a fixed draw. Exact computation removes Monte Carlo
error, not population uncertainty. MTLD variants also differ in direction
averaging, threshold and trailing-factor rules. Compare measurements only after
aligning formulas, parameters and segmentation; regenerate historical reports
when those contracts changed. See [formula and guard details](METHODS.md#6-lexical-diversity-indices).

### Linguistic proxies and literary interpretation

Analysis shares a bounded Markdown prose projection. Link labels contribute;
destinations, images, code, comments and excluded document regions do not.
Paragraph profiles preserve displayed text and source anchors separately from
counting. The configured token rules and narrower paragraph scope do not imply
complete CommonMark support or linguistic token accuracy. See
[analysis scope](METHODS.md) for the unit and denominator of each measurement.

Passive, tense, adjective, nominalization and modality fields count lexical
markers or suffixes. For example, German `werden` also marks future tense or
becoming; English `been` also appears in active perfect constructions. These
counts do not identify syntactic voice or distinguish epistemic uncertainty
from obligation. Sentence segmentation and syllables are also heuristic;
utterance abbreviations (`no.`, `co.`) split sentences and tokenless
fragments do not count as sentences.
Suffix cues over-include on purpose-ambiguous words: English nominal `-th`
counts *month/health/truth*, German adjective `-ig`/`-al` count
*König/Saal*, German nominal `-ik`/`-ur` count *Musik/Natur*. Modal lexicons
have unequal morphology coverage (German and Dutch include preterite forms,
the other profiles only present), so `modal_density` is not comparable across
languages.

Readability coefficient tests verify the declared formulas, not their original
calibration or reader comprehension. Amstad's original coefficient page and
calibration protocol have not been verified here. Scores may fall outside 0–100
and are not comparable across language formulas. [German PALME research
(2026)](https://aclanthology.org/2026.bea-1.6/) separates controlled detector tests
from graded-reader evaluation; its results do not validate Lixity's regex cues.

Showing/telling is a composite of those visible signals. Empty rankings and
zero fallback scores do not establish equal artistic effect. Without explicit
dividers, pacing scenes are chapter placeholders. Short sentences, perception
verbs and vocabulary contrast do not establish immersion, tension or a reason
to rewrite. Scene/register targets are explicit author preferences, never
hardcoded genre norms. [Underwood's expert discussion](https://tedunderwood.com/2024/01/05/can-language-models-predict-the-next-twist-in-a-story/)
illustrates why surface predictability and narrative experience differ.

Dialogue turns are quotation segments without speaker attribution. Character
mentions depend on supplied names or literal project aliases; declared viewpoint
chapters are separate metadata, not inferred first-person presence. There is no
NER or coreference. Hook and repetition scores also locate surface patterns;
deliberate calm endings and repeated motifs can be appropriate author choices.

### Structural diagnostics

These diagnostics preserve their declared numerical definitions; an exact
implementation does not validate the underlying model:

- `pelt_changepoints` uses exact unpruned dynamic programming: $O(n^2)$
  time and $O(n)$ storage. The retained singleton/zero-variance guard violates
  the PELT pruning premise, so no pruning or linear-time claim is made.
  Anchored variance updates reduce cancellation; exact optimization of this
  guarded objective does not validate its Gaussian model or a narrative break.
  [Killick et al., Theorem 3.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.1438v3).
- Sn uses the original low outer/high inner medians and factor 1.1926. Qn
  preserves its pairwise-distance rank with modern factor 2.21914; neither
  applies finite-sample correction. Normal-consistency factors, finite bias
  corrections and robustness remain distinct. [Original paper](https://wis.kuleuven.be/stat/robust/papers/publications-1993/rousseeuwcroux-alternativestomedianad-jasa-1993.pdf),
  [maintained reference](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/robustbase/robustbase.pdf).
- Early/late Wasserstein integrates the exact empirical-CDF difference;
  merged CDFs also give KS $D$, with $D=0$ returning $p=1$ and stable survival
  evaluation. The same asymptotic probability model remains: ties, short
  samples, serial dependence and fitted distributions are not calibrated by
  this numerical correction. Mann–Kendall `tau` remains tau-a, with a
  tie-corrected approximate normal probability for $S$, not tau-b.
- The graph exponent follows the approximate discrete estimator in
  [Clauset–Shalizi–Newman Eq. 3.7](https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.1062v2).
  The current continuous fitted CDF and ordinary KS probability do not implement
  its refitted goodness-of-fit procedure. Graph degrees are dependent too;
  neither a fit distance nor a small sample certifies a scale-free graph.

Early/late splits are chapter-count midpoints, not learned narrative boundaries.
Signed Dunning keyness ranks token contrast; it has no multiplicity adjustment.
Chapter-to-rest JSD is raw divergence in nats, not its square-root distance or
an external Delta authorship test. Inspect driver words in context. Formula
details and unchanged field contracts: [METHODS §4c](METHODS.md#4c-structural-diagnostics-structural_diagnostics).

**Accessibility / data visualisation (WCAG 2.2).**
- Colour must never be the only channel (SC 1.4.1, 1.3.3): the heatmap
  prints the numeric z* values, the band chart encodes band/median/outliers
  by position and shape, every chip reveals tense + value as text on click.
- Contrast targets are 3:1 for relevant non-text UI and 4.5:1 for normal text.
  Lixity chooses heatmap text from each cell’s luminance and
  tests the full blue/orange scale. This does not certify every canvas mark or
  every color-vision condition; numeric labels remain essential.
- WCAG 2.5.8 has a 24×24 CSS-pixel minimum with defined exceptions. Paragraph
  chips and dimension controls use at least 24×24,
  increasing to 44×44 for coarse pointers. Pressed chips retain their target
  size, and long strips scroll horizontally. These checks do not establish
  conformance for the entire interface or every canvas mark.
- Diverging scales have a meaningful midpoint: zero deviation from the
  within-manuscript reference (median in the robust style calculation).
- See [visual design rationale](ARCHITECTURE.md#visual-consistency-and-evidence)
  for evidence, typography choices and the limits of automated UI checks.

## 2. Stability register

The current cross-cutting limits below replace the completed-bug checklist.
Historical fixes and release-specific evidence remain in [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/mfahsold/lixity/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md),
[release notes](https://github.com/mfahsold/lixity/tree/main/docs/releases) and the
[archived register and verification snapshot](https://github.com/mfahsold/lixity/blob/123b198db2b3d276b4bba71664e4e6b989377247/docs/STABILITY.md#2-stability-register).

| Surface | Remaining boundary | Maintained reference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Numerical reproducibility | Floating-point last bits can differ across interpreters/platforms. | [Methods](METHODS.md) |
| Large dashboards | Bundled assets and full offline text increase document size; opening paragraph details lazily does not remove the retained text payload. | [Architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md) |
| Workspace status | File-derived status is advisory; timestamps and restored files can be misleading. Unknown is not success. | [Workspace interfaces](AGENTS.md) |
| Optional project adapters | Core checks do not verify a project's launcher, export tools or local runtime. | [Installation](INSTALLATION.md) |
| Publication formats | Font coverage and layout limits remain; no EPUB, PDF/UA or PDF/X certification is claimed. | [PDF export](USAGE.md#download-a-manuscript-pdf) |
| Agreement drafts | Built-in PDF fonts do not cover every script; download text for external rendering and retain reviewed documents in project storage. | [Project interface](AGENTS.md) |

Empty optional signal fields, unavailable small-sample metrics and missing
rankings must be interpreted using their configuration/availability metadata.
They are not evidence of no signal or equal literary effect.

===============================================================================
## docs/LOCALIZATION.md

Source: https://github.com/mfahsold/lixity/blob/main/docs/LOCALIZATION.md

# Language and localization contract

## Defaults and developer language

Documentation, comments and docstrings are English. Localized resources,
quoted material and linguistic examples retain their intended language.
Machine-readable keys and mathematical identifiers remain language-neutral.

Analysis language and report language are separate settings:

| Setting | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `--language de`, `--language en`, or another supported code | Selects the manuscript's linguistic profile. An explicit CLI flag overrides project settings; English is the default. API callers use the `language` argument. |
| `--language auto` | Requests detection explicitly. Weak or ambiguous evidence resolves to `generic`. |
| `LIXITY_LANG` | Selects CLI/report presentation independently of analysis. Message packs currently cover German and English. |
| Dashboard language | Uses resources for all seven supported languages, including workspace and research controls. |

Detection uses the text the caller supplies: `pipeline.resolve_document_config`
resolves `auto` before analysis. Low-level `CorpusAnalyzer`/`ParagraphProfiler`
calls resolve `auto` without a sample and fall back to `generic`, so resolve
`auto` first (or pass a concrete key) before calling them directly.

Research CLI help and errors are English; JSON keys are language-neutral.
Sources, quotations, filenames, external metadata, claim titles and author
decisions are preserved as entered. Localization does not translate or verify
research content. Some backend errors may still appear in English in the browser.

## Localization below the interface

Supported profiles are German (`de`), English (`en`), French (`fr`), Spanish
(`es`), Italian (`it`), Portuguese (`pt`) and Dutch (`nl`). German and English
currently have the most extensive linguistic heuristics and language-specific
fixtures. The other five profiles have localized presentation and linguistic
resources with more limited coverage and validation. Equal interface coverage
does not establish equal accuracy across languages or genres.

| Concern | What changes with the language |
| --- | --- |
| Words and sentences | Word patterns, abbreviations and sentence-boundary rules (sentence boundaries never cross blank lines) |
| Tense and style signals | Present/past markers, function words, pronouns, modality, passive and nominal patterns |
| Readability | Syllable estimation and the named language-specific coefficient set |
| Presentation | Labels, scientific explanations, decimal/grouping separators and percentage units |
| Generic profile | Reduced fallback heuristics, not a validated model for an unknown language |

OCR badges resolve stable diagnostic codes through the same workspace label
packs. `ready` describes configuration, not recognition quality. Source URLs
and quotations are never translated. See [research limits](research/USAGE.md).

## Mathematics and scientific interpretation

Median/MAD normalization, measurement-error adjustment, multiple-testing
correction and eigendecomposition use the same mathematics in every language.
Translation must not change these numerical results. Their linguistic inputs
can differ; cross-language scores are not automatically comparable. JSON
numbers stay numeric; locale formatting applies only to displayed reports.

Readability coefficients are documented in [Methods](METHODS.md). Results are
not clipped to 0–100 and do not diagnose literary quality. The generic profile
uses fallback coefficients, not a model calibrated for every language.

Syllable counts, tense classification and stylistic patterns are deterministic
heuristics, not a full grammatical parser. Dialect, historical spelling,
code-switching and unusual vocabulary need separate evaluation.
German and English default word patterns include precomposed accented words;
they do not normalize Unicode or cover every combining-mark spelling. Explicit
word patterns retain their own flags. Hyphenated compounds stay one token under
the German and English defaults and split under the other five profiles;
apostrophes remain word-internal there. Syllable calculation reuses word
frequencies within a request, preserving the same heuristic values without a
global cache.

v0.7.2 corrects the five profiles' internal-apostrophe patterns for both `'` and
`’`. First-person sentence-start matching treats these two forms alike without
changing the original token used for starter diversity or the manuscript text.
These are orthographic counting conventions, not grammatical segmentation of
clitics. Recompute affected token-based and sentence-start results before
comparing reports from earlier versions.

The German v0.7.2 perception/filter list also adds finite indicative present and
simple-past forms of *hören* and *riechen*. Neutral positive and negative fixtures
cover shared corpus/chapter/paragraph/scene counting and explicit overrides.
This does not validate perception, grammatical roles or all German inflections;
see [the cue-list limits](METHODS.md#perceptionfilter-word-cues).

## Acceptance criteria for language work

Prioritize German linguistic resources and scientific explanations, then English,
then the other supported languages. Documentation remains English; this priority
does not change the default analysis language or imply equal validation.

1. Supply and test linguistic resources; do not substitute English patterns.
2. Provide complete, nonempty label/help keys and review translation quality.
3. Document formula sources and unavailable analyses; do not invent coefficients.
4. Test known numeric examples and language-specific positive/negative fixtures.
5. Apply locale formatting only when displaying results; keep JSON numbers numeric.
6. Distinguish coverage and dispatch tests from empirical validation.

`tests/test_localization.py` checks defaults, explicit detection, resource keys,
coefficient selection and number formatting. Linguistic and mathematical suites
add specific examples. Together, they do not establish a language-wide accuracy
percentage.

**Since v0.7.3:** contextual action help, the visible keyboard
reference and internal-reference descriptions use the same seven UI label packs.
Browser checks cover pack/placeholder parity, document language, real source
toolbars and reading controls at desktop and narrow widths. Full translated
sentences are kept intact; technical key names and identifiers stay stable.
These checks establish coverage and layout, not a professional translation review
or equal linguistic-analysis accuracy across the seven languages.

===============================================================================
## docs/ARCHITECTURE.md

Source: https://github.com/mfahsold/lixity/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md

# Architecture and integration boundaries

This document records shared responsibilities and integration boundaries.
Product maturity, response schemas and research storage versions are independent.
[Usage](USAGE.md) owns workflows; [automation](AGENTS.md) owns request and result
contracts; [research usage](research/USAGE.md) describes implemented archive behavior.
The [research RFC](research/README.md) includes unimplemented proposals.

`lixity.research` owns explicit-project captures, immutable snapshots, citations,
authored records and a rebuildable SQLite/FTS5 index. It does not import into
`lixity.pipeline`. Source analysis may use the shared engine and UI, but research
sources never join manuscript baselines automatically.

The [local data model](research/DATA_MODEL.md) diagrams the current reference
chain and publication process, and separates authoritative archive data from
the disposable search database. Historical interchange proposals do not define
the accepted local schema.

## Layers

| Layer | Responsibility | Must not own |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Language resources | Lexicons, patterns, labels, formula coefficients | Project-specific character lists or file paths |
| Analysis core | Metrics, paragraph profiles, uncertainty and statistical diagnostics | HTTP sessions, exports or UI state |
| `lixity.pipeline` | Resolve document language; assemble one analysis result | Implicit file reads or mutable global project state |
| CLI / `lixity.api` | Input/output contracts and threshold resolution | Duplicate analysis algorithms |
| UI | Render results using shared components and bundled assets | Recompute statistical decisions in JavaScript |
| `publication` / `pdf_export` | Validate entered publication data; compose shared PDF bytes | Infer legal identities, establish rights or write output files |
| `lixity.server` | Loopback transport, request guards, one shared dashboard assembly and selected-workspace transitions | A second renderer, a second analysis path or CLI/service lifecycles |
| `config` / `io` / `workspace` | Explicit project metadata, atomic byte I/O and manuscript discovery | Implicit identity/publication defaults or duplicate writers |
| `lixity.service` | Managed local process lifecycle (start/stop/restart/status) | Adopting externally managed units |
| Project adapters | Manuscript access, publication actions and local services | Copies of the engine |

`lixity.math_core` is the single mathematical vocabulary of the analysis core
(robust scale, significance z, normal tail, ratio/share/density totalization,
plug-in standard errors and published effect bands). Heuristics import it
instead of restating formulas; `style_fingerprint` re-exports the historical
names for callers.

The server separates transport (`runtime`, `_base`, `handler`), selected-workspace
state (`_state`), dashboard assembly (`views`) and domain route groups. Registered
route tables drive dispatch and discovery. Handlers validate and shape requests,
then delegate to the shared pipeline or `research.api`; they do not implement a
second renderer, analysis algorithm or archive writer.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    T[CLI and Python API] --> P[Shared analysis pipeline]
    S[Native server routes] --> P
    P --> A[Analysis core and language resources]
    P --> R[Shared report and dashboard renderers]
    S --> Q[Explicit-project research API]
    T --> Q
    Q --> J[Authoritative revision and blob repository]
    J --> C[Rebuildable SQLite search projection]
    Q --> R
```

Arrows show delegation or derivation, not a second analysis or storage path.
Research measurements use the same core only when explicitly requested; retained
source passages do not enter manuscript baselines. The browser owns transient
selection/display state, while guarded routes delegate durable writes to the
research API and repository.

One process has one selected workspace. Opening selects an existing project;
importing browser bytes creates one at an explicit destination. A browser filename
does not identify its original parent directory. An archive may open without a
manuscript. `workspace.resolve_project_target` resolves explicit selectors; API
research calls stay explicitly scoped. An occupied port fails startup. Since
v0.7.2, an invalid explicit `serve` selector fails before binding or selecting a
workspace. Valid directories without a unique manuscript can still open as empty
workspaces; `--no-project` explicitly starts without project selection.

`DocumentAnalysis` reuses corpus/chapter measurements for the fingerprint and
renderers. Narrower profile/fingerprint requests use the same pipeline. Dashboard
refresh validates manuscript bytes before serving cached measurements and rebuilds
when a readable changed source can be rendered. **Since v0.7.2:**
`RefreshOutcome` distinguishes unchanged/rebuilt, missing, unreadable and failed
refreshes. Missing/unreadable sources and config/render failures retain the last
successful HTML, metadata and source digest, with a per-response localized
freshness notice and a plain GET retry route. They do not relabel old measurements
with an unvalidated source identity. Recovery after a failed rebuild requires a
successful rebuild; recovery from a read outage can validate identical bytes
without recomputing. Explicit analyze/rebuild requests fail when the selected
source is unavailable. No versioned JSON fields or automatic configuration
watcher are added. Research overviews reuse one validated archive snapshot without
a persistent cache.

Plain inline prose uses the existing markup cleaner directly when it contains
none of the escape, code or link openers. Syntax-bearing input retains the same
delimiter recognizer; the optimization changes neither the counting projection
nor exact source/display identities. Language profiles own word boundaries;
first-person matching normalizes apostrophe variants only in its comparison key,
leaving source text and starter-diversity tokens intact.

Research backup export and restoration share complete manifest-chain validation
in `research.archive`: bounded, checksum-verified objects must satisfy the
versioned manifest model, project identity, consecutive generations and root
termination. Invalid or incomplete history fails before output replacement or
restored-store publication. Inventory paths use the repository's existing
containment/symlink boundary, which also rejects parent components. This is
validation of the existing format, with no schema migration or alternate store.

**Since v0.7.3:** export owns the repository writer lock from
accepted-snapshot selection until its compressed candidate is self-contained.
This serializes commits and purge against the copied records/blobs. Root pointers
come from that snapshot; stored object content addresses and the bytes actually
copied must agree. The candidate is flushed before output replacement. A failure
before replacement preserves the previous backup; a later directory-sync failure
reports published output with uncertain durability. Restore validates envelope
shape, identifiers, digests and optional sizes before inventory reads, rejecting
duplicate members. Export format and canonical records remain unchanged.

## Manual manuscript associations

`research.manuscript` owns `ManuscriptClaimLink`, separate from imported source
evidence. Explicitly permitted quote retention pins a reviewed claim revision and
an immutable `paragraph-profile-text/1` anchor: project-relative path, source and
displayed-paragraph hashes, source lines and Unicode-codepoint offsets. The first
opted-in save requires record/manifest v7; reads never upgrade existing archives.
Historical v3.0.1 supports only v1–v6 despite its higher product number.

`pipeline.paragraph_identity` supplies the same identity to rendering and research.
`FileUtils.read_source_snapshot` binds raw bytes and decoded text; creation checks
source containment and bytes again before publication. Review uses the validated
archive snapshot and existing pipeline paragraphs. It preserves anchors and claim
pins, distinguishes missing from unreadable sources, and leaves ambiguous or moved
candidates for explicit review. It does not infer factual support.

Manuscript routes validate both selected manuscript and archive contexts before
calling the API. Saved-quote counts join explicit associations from one coherent
snapshot, disclose differing revision pins and do not establish manuscript use or
nonuse. Rendering preserves exact resolved quote spans and complete text search.

**Since v0.7.2:** relation navigation opens an association's pinned
claim revision, then its explicit pinned dossier reference. Scoped Review routes
join saved manuscript associations by those references, independently of the
dossier's derived current-claim list. Only existing exact anchor matches offer
passage jumps. The document origin/return context is ephemeral and guarded by the
current project/source/research context. Its compact work thread displays the
original chapter/line span and the last accepted viewed record identity and saved
revision, distinguishing an explicitly pinned version from a current or viewed
version. Return or a changed project/source/research context clears the thread;
no archive/backend schema is introduced.
Native selection uses ephemeral paragraph-local UTF-16 offsets and direction,
rebuilt against exact paragraph text on return so annotation repaint cannot
mutate a saved live Range. Saved archive offsets remain Unicode codepoints. Existing citation
envelopes retain source version, passage identity, hashes and offsets. Ordinary
source reading is not relabelled as the historical cited version. Retained quote
cards do not provide a full historical-source reader. Dossier readers group
authored notes, derived current-linked claims and citations, while global claims
and decisions remain available through their existing routes.

Ordinary authored CLI updates require a reviewed revision, change kind and reason;
when the archive snapshot is omitted, the backend's current read guards the same
strict writer. Changed associations require reviewed pins; races fail without retry.
`research.revisions` shares candidate validation across exact writes,
dry runs and batch preparation. Prospective comparison uses one snapshot for both
values; historical comparison resolves saved revisions without repinning. Section
reconciliation changes only the selected body subtree while ordinary field changes
use the same candidate. HTTP, images, acknowledgements and batches retain their
explicit guards. No preview establishes that a future write will succeed.

Since v0.7.2, normalized authored content equality is decided in
`research.revisions` after complete metadata, field and association validation.
An unchanged candidate returns the exact prior record, preserving its revision,
encoding and historical pins. Mixed batches publish changed members only; invalid
operations reject the entire batch. `research.repository` retains the writer
lock and concurrent HEAD check even for an empty commit, then returns without
rewriting retained bytes, HEAD or the disposable SQLite index. Immutable JSON
records, blobs, manifests and HEAD remain authoritative; no archive migration or
second store is introduced. Decision acknowledgements remain append-only events,
not authored-content no-ops.

`research.dossier_edit` encodes an explicit leading JSON comment and
the exact body as a Markdown draft. It validates identity/base and delegates to
existing three-way preparation; ready changes become ordinary batch operations.
Versioned reviewed packets bind project and snapshot through the shared backend.
The archive stays authoritative: there is no parallel store, watcher or two-way
sync. Exports use exclusive publication outside the archive/internal directory.
The canonical project writer lock remains the only mutex; diagnostic error types
distinguish contention, read-only/permission failures and other I/O errors.

### Passage research presentation

**Since v0.7.3:** `manuscript-links.js` selects exact saved
associations with the same resolved lines, paragraph hash, codepoint span and
quotation matcher used for manuscript marks. Explicit paragraph activation
composes existing GETs for pinned claim/dossier records and current dossier
decision reviews; it adds no endpoint or archive schema. The first five
associations and first five decisions per displayed dossier have explicit totals.
Current dossier context is distinct from the historical claim/dossier pins.

This composition stays in the existing link closure, with its root, project,
source and review-generation guards. Duplicate exact reads coalesce within an
activation; inconsistent snapshot envelopes fail instead of mixing versions.
`LixityWorkbench` owns the `research` context tool alongside values and dossier,
and `LixityReadingThread` owns the exact passage return. Opening a context neither
replaces the prose node nor saves records. Unlinked text, an uninitialized archive,
unavailable data and failed/stale reads have distinct states. The public demo
uses the same static website projection and read-only profile as exported
project reading copies.

### Static reading websites

`site_export.prepare_site` reads an explicit project and assembles a bounded
`SiteBundle`. Review mode uses the shared pipeline and `render_analysis`, with
the native UI's read-only capabilities. Its research data is a separate opt-in
projection of one verified snapshot; original source files and full extraction
text require another opt-in. Snapshot-scoped native response helpers avoid
repeatedly loading the archive. No global cross-request archive cache or relaxed
corruption check is involved.

Reader and companion modes resolve a validated root `site_publications` profile
against that snapshot. They select current or explicitly pinned dossier versions,
unique heading subtrees, public titles and chapter release gates before rendering.
They never serialize native Research responses or calculate manuscript analysis.
Whole-dossier citations and geography require explicit profile fields; images and
source bytes require a separate, one-export choice. Reverse associations, internal
claims, decisions and history are not inferred publication selections.

An export cap removes later entries and dependency assets before serialization;
reader mode additionally truncates canonical manuscript chapters and omits markers,
front matter and appendices. Companion mode passes no manuscript blocks to the
shared reading shell. Both reuse the literal ReaderBlock renderer and native
Markdown, diagram, image and geographic components. Browser-local progress is an
explicit reading aid, scoped to publication identity, source hash and cap. It does
not establish access rights: included later bytes remain inspectable. Invalid or
unavailable storage starts at chapter zero, and preview never advances progress.

The embedded `lixity-read-only-site-data/1` response table contains enumerated
prepared reads. The first-loaded static transport returns these reads without
a server, rejects mutation and unknown requests, and never falls back to a
host's `/api`. Shared UI owners suppress unsupported editing and administrative
actions. Retained media uses explicit bundled-resource mappings; maps start
with offline geometry, without external tiles or implicit analytics requests.
Browser-local reading preferences remain available.

`export_site` publishes a fresh directory only after complete assembly; existing
destinations are rejected. The native `site-export` route downloads an in-memory
ZIP, bound to the current manuscript metadata token and rechecked selection.
It does not publish a site or create files in the source project. The website
manifest inventories scope, source identities and file digests. It is a public
projection contract, separate from archive entity/manifest versions; it does
not supply accounts, encryption, copy prevention or a restorable backup. See
[the data model](research/DATA_MODEL.md#reading-website-projection) and
[the sharing workflow](USAGE.md#export-a-reading-website).

## Configuration and multiple projects

Explicit root settings own author identity, publication, reading-site profiles,
chapter registers and project-local character profiles; user/ancestor defaults cannot supply them.
The optional root `manuscript` setting follows the same project-only boundary.
`config.read_explicit_project_config` reuses the existing TOML parser but reads
only root pyproject/lixity files and promotes failed reads to errors.
The native view, PDF composer and website exporter all use this selected root,
including when the manuscript is in a subdirectory with another configuration.
`workspace.configured_manuscript` owns contained relative-path resolution without
reading source bytes. `discover` applies explicit → configured → conventional
selection and validates configured regular files. The read-only Research CLI
uses the same path owner after validating its archive, then preserves its domain
review of missing/unreadable source bytes. Python text-analysis APIs stay explicit.

**Since v0.7.3:** `workspace.resolve_manuscript_target` selects
one root/source pair before analysis configuration is loaded. Command-level
`--project` and root-configured omission use strict root-local settings; legacy
explicit files and conventional scenes/build discovery without `--project`
retain their existing merge. The Research CLI normalizes omitted manuscript
input after validating its archive. These selectors do not change a running server's project or any JSON
result encoding.
Output scene filters run after complete measurement; explicitly planned IDs remain
separate from measured rows and never influence descriptive baselines.

`project_identity` compares only bounded
manuscript metadata syntax, without rewriting text or affecting measurements.
`PublicationSettings`/`PUBLICATION_FIELDS` supply field validation to configuration,
settings and PDF composition. `pdf_export.compose_pdf` composes bytes for CLI and
HTTP; callers own output writes. Front matter uses entered data, and syntax checks
do not establish publication compliance.

Since v0.7.0, manuscript PDFs use one presentation projection
(`manuscript_document`) of the shared Markdown blocks. It retains structure and readable
inline styles rather than using the statistical prose filter. Book, editorial
and submission layouts share block placement and the same PDF document engine;
the analysis report retains its metric tables. Editorial geometry reuses
`BookLayoutConfig`, which also remains available to embedding adapters.

`config.prepare_project_settings` validates one settings candidate while
preserving unrelated TOML values. The route renders that candidate,
commits through `PreparedProjectSettings`, then publishes session/cache state.
Decode, validation, render or replacement failures publish none of the candidate.
Selected-context tokens bind source/root and both root config digests. Publication/
register saves and manuscript PDF downloads reject stale required context. Config
reads accept regular nonsymlink files and verify the opened descriptor's identity.
The optimistic commit guard checks observed identity and bytes immediately before
replacement; it is neither an external-editor lock nor a manuscript content pin.

**Since v0.6.0:** explicitly requested language/threshold defaults
reuse this transaction and its project token. Session-only Apply remains the
default. Installed configuration metadata derives publication bounds from the
same model/field registry used by rendering and validation.

`FileUtils.atomic_write_bytes_if_changed` is the shared text/binary writer:
same-directory staging, complete write, flush, mode preservation, fsync and atomic
replacement. Unchanged bytes skip replacement and its optional guard. Errors
propagate, temporary stages are cleaned, and no direct-overwrite fallback exists.
`Workspace.publish` preserves distinct same-minute artifacts, recognizes historical
archive names and prepares the stable artifact before replacement. Failure stops
before archive rotation.

`load_project_config(path)` searches from its supplied path and merges supported
project/user settings. Pass the intended mapping to `resolve_document_config` and
`resolve_thresholds`; explicit options win. An empty mapping selects code defaults
without discovery. The facade's `profile`, `fingerprint`/`passport` and `dashboard`
accept that mapping; `None` retains threshold discovery for compatibility.
Use `analyze_document(text, config, thresholds)` when several outputs need the same
measurements. Project adapters own their characters, motifs, paths and artifacts.

Shared owners preserve failure signals across interfaces: configuration discovery
reports metadata/read failures and malformed TOML sections through its existing
warning channel; the guarded `FileUtils` source reader also serves dialogue,
pacing, motifs and showing CLI commands. Low-level structure reports reuse the
English `CorpusConfig` default, while explicit `auto` retains detection.
`StyleFingerprint.from_metrics` rejects non-finite feature values and invalid
standard errors before scoring; documented unavailable-value conventions remain
separate. Research claim-confidence and evidence-relation normalization belongs
to `research.api`; supplied invalid HTTP values fail rather than receiving an
omission default.

The shared Markdown parser defines measurement prose and chapter numbering.
Inline counting retains visible link labels and excludes link targets,
images and code. It stays separate from displayed paragraph text and quote identity;
zero-token chapters retain their source numbering. `characters.CharacterProfile`
owns literal alias/declared-POV validation and its discoverable schema; one resolver
serves CLI, API and dashboard. Declared POV stays separate from lexical mention counts.
Paragraph profiles cover body/list blocks; legacy whitespace counts remain
separate. Token regex flags are preserved, while linguistic cue patterns have a
case-insensitive compiler. [Methods](METHODS.md) defines exact scopes and numerical
conventions. Scene groups compare only explicitly assigned manuscript observations.

Research revision preparation, section edits and grouped saves reuse strict
validation and one repository commit. Section reads, preparation and image placement
share the code-aware ATX heading parser. Review follows recorded links and revision
pins, without inferring contradictions. Images reuse immutable source/version/blob
records, never fabricated text passages; textual analysis rejects them. Attachment
and dossier revision publish atomically. Purge retains identity for honest unavailable
placeholders, not image bytes. Shared limits come from `research.limits`.

## Presentation and trust boundaries

The dashboard is a self-contained HTML file. Python bundles CSS and scripts; no
CDN or frontend build step is required. Chapter-title tooltips use text nodes,
not executable markup. Rendering and point picking share projected coordinates. Animation
is scheduled only while rotation is enabled and the page is visible. The live
shell applies a per-response script nonce and default-deny CSP; bundled components
require no `unsafe-eval`.

Research media reuse bundled PhotoSwipe 5.4.4 for retained images and
generated diagrams. Mermaid tiny 12.2.0 owns diagram syntax/layout and initializes
only when a diagram first becomes visible; restrictions disable resource loading,
click actions and configuration directives, with source retained on failure.
Leaflet 1.9.4 provides geographic vectors. **Since v0.7.2:** visible
maps load OpenStreetMap tiles by default; users can turn off the background or
choose the offline sketch. Tile requests stop outside the visible map/project
context. Tiles reveal the client IP and viewed area;
attached historical images remain independent evidence, not calibrated basemaps.

### Logging

`src/lixity/log.py` is the one logging entry point. Modules log through
`get_logger()` under the `lixity` tree; the CLI keeps stdout as its result
channel and sends diagnostics through logging. Lines use a single UTC format
(`YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS UTC LEVEL lixity.<area> message`) with standard levels,
resolved from an explicit argument, else `LIXITY_LOG_LEVEL`, else DEBUG while
`LIXITY_DEBUG`/`--debug` is active, else INFO.

The managed service appends the child's stderr to `service-PORT.log`;
`rotate_service_log()` bounds that file at service start (one writer per file,
rotated to `.1`–`.3`). The stderr handler follows `sys.stderr` at emit time,
so `redirect_stderr`, the captured service descriptor and tests all see the
same stream. Request logs never contain query strings — context tokens and
selectors travel there — and log records never contain manuscript text.

`ui/dimensions.py` renders a semantic score table from the same measured points
as the canvas. It keeps chapter titles, available scores and native chapter links
usable without JavaScript; native rotation/zoom controls call the same projection
renderer. Unmeasured chapters and absent axes are omitted.

### Visual consistency and evidence

The local dashboard and Pages share `ui/assets/design-tokens.css`; components and
surface styles own actual color, typography, spacing and control rules. Heatmap
text selects contrast from cell luminance. Native controls, visible boundaries,
focus outlines and non-color cues support navigation. [WCAG contrast](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html),
[target size](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html)
and [text-spacing overrides](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/text-spacing.html)
inform the checks; defaults are product choices, not universal typographic optima.
Exact tokens and dimensions belong to CSS and executable checks rather than a
second prose specification.

**Since v0.7.3:** prose heading roles cover all six Markdown
levels; subordinate headings do not fall through to small browser defaults.
Fenced code inherits its block's size instead of compounding inline-code scaling.
Shared controls inherit the interface font; canvas labels resolve the same UI and
technical font tokens through the existing style probe. Serif manuscript text,
system interface text and monospace technical notation remain distinct roles.
[Fluent typography guidance](https://fluent2.microsoft.design/typography) informs
this role-based hierarchy. [Wallace et al. (2022)](https://research.adobe.com/publication/towards-individuated-reading-experiences-different-fonts-increase-reading-speed-for-different-individuals/)
found individual differences in font-related reading performance; that does not
establish one best font or a reading-speed benefit for Lixity.

The manuscript is the primary workspace. Analysis supports passage selection
and interpretation; retained evidence and authored dossiers provide context.
These are connected views over the same project, not independent products.

**Since v0.7.2:** interactive dashboards use a fixed project sidebar
on wide screens, with manuscript/analysis first, research second and settings
third. Narrow screens keep a horizontal switcher. Tab orientation and keyboard
navigation change together; the sidebar scrolls independently if its controls
exceed the viewport. Plain exported reports retain their document layout.
Both presentations use the same renderer, labels, data and action handlers.
The desktop navigation uses the shared `ctl` toggle. Companion reading applies a
temporary collapse override only in the analysis view; closing restores the manual
choice. Responsive changes keep the mobile switcher available. Exact manuscript
return actions reuse the existing paragraph navigation and the same anchor matcher
as inline association marks, with a current project/source context check on click.

**Since v0.7.3:** the native shell renders the product row,
primary destinations, project identity, project actions and secondary version/
license information in that DOM order. Navigation no longer depends on runtime
reparenting. App chrome uses interface typography; exported document headers keep
their existing presentation. The shared collapse owner hides project context and
actions while retaining product identity and all three destinations.

### Shared manuscript reader

**Since v0.7.2:** `ui/manuscript_reader.py` emits the shared command
surface. The interactive manuscript stays continuous while an **Analysis** toggle
exposes diagnostic presentation in place. Turning the layer on does not open a
dock or apply the navigation-collapse override. Its absolute gutter marker does
not consume prose width or change line wrapping. The constant accessible name,
pressed state, switch indicator and visible On/Off text distinguish that choice
from the active context tool; the state label reserves enough width for either
localized value. Dense comparisons use an overview with a return to the preserved
passage and prior overlay choice. There is one
canonical manuscript DOM; changing tools or analysis visibility does not replace
its source text or create a hidden duplicate reading tree. Loaded-project chrome
uses a class emitted by the renderer; it does not use a body-level `:has` query
over the mutable prose tree, which would broaden annotation/style invalidation.
When the leading authored level-one heading exactly matches the project title,
the reading surface suppresses only the generated sidebar title. The original
source heading stays intact, and Project, Research and the analysis overview keep
the generated project context. The existing workbench owner publishes the view
attribute; no prose observer or second navigation state is introduced.

Exact analysis evidence in v0.7.3 is a separate optional projection, collected
inside the existing paragraph-profile pass. `ParagraphMatcher` owns the same
resolved counters used for profiles and literal evidence; the UI does not run a
parallel linguistic detector. `DocumentAnalysis.evidence` is not part of default
analysis/profile JSON. The renderer appends its paragraph-identity envelope to
existing lazy paragraph data. Native CSS Highlight ranges preserve the prose DOM;
a single Preact leaf owns the explanation card. Only visible paragraph generations
are prepared, with explicit codepoint-to-UTF-16 conversion and hash validation.
Search/research mark changes invalidate derived ranges, not source identities.
Analysis visibility, metric changes and workspace changes cancel stale cards and
marks. Unsupported or unprovable mappings remain explicit unavailable states.
Since v0.7.4, the paragraph menu opens one existing passage inspector. Its
measurement action captures the source point and uses the evidence owner; its
research action delegates to the existing explicit passage association reader.
An identical accepted manuscript-review report in the same source/project
context retains its list nodes, preserving native dialog focus-return targets.
A changed report or list filter still renders; errors clear the accepted report.
The presentation keeps computed counts and authored research separate without
a new context state or transport contract. The floating card uses native counts
and the existing paragraph comparison; it never parses localized numeric text.

The existing reader preferences also retain the selected metric and marking
choice. First explicit Analysis On defaults to `asl` only without a saved choice;
the native disclosure beside the switch contains the single existing selector
and marking checkbox. Explicit paragraph inspection can enable Analysis through
the workbench owner while preserving disabled paint. Missing cryptographic
verification is distinguished from a mismatching paragraph identity.

The existing paragraph menu snapshots a native pointer caret as a transient
UTF-16 paragraph offset and evidence identity. After normal source verification,
inspection selects the existing counted span containing that point; it does not
run another detector or guess a quotation after reflow. Ellipsis and keyboard
actions without a literal pointer point keep the first-match entry. A transient
opening token cancels superseded requests across the reader's layout wait while
allowing its own position restoration; explicit pointer, wheel, scroll-key and
view/layer changes take precedence.

`manuscript_document.manuscript_blocks` supplies source-ordered semantic blocks
with absolute inclusive line spans, before PDF-specific title suppression and
endnote movement. Its existing `manuscript_sections` adapter retains the strict
PDF inline/TeX contract. `ui.manuscript_document.reader_blocks` joins source blocks
to existing `ParagraphProfile` owners by interval, preserving each original
`p-N`, exact text, hash and source span. One profile can cover several presentation
list items; that profile remains a single owner. Partial overlaps retain uncovered
source lines literally, while overlapping profile owners fail explicitly.

Source-holding API, CLI, native and retained-source render paths pass the optional
presentation to the same dashboard renderer. Profile-only callers retain their
existing fallback. Preface, empty chapters, supported headings/quotes/code/dividers/
notes and the analysis-excluded appendix remain readable without acquiring
statistical coverage. Unprofiled blocks have no invented values or claim-writing
actions. Pipe tables and unsupported inline syntax stay literal; HTML/TeX-looking
text is escaped, and manuscript images are not fetched automatically. In
particular, rich link/footnote normalization cannot change the existing exact
paragraph-text quotation contract. This is a bounded source presentation, not
a new editor, general Markdown engine or analysis JSON schema.

The reader uses native buttons, selects and disclosures with shared `ctl` styles
and the seven-language label pack. Size, width, spacing and split preferences live
in browser storage; denied or malformed storage falls back to usable defaults.
Focus mode is reversible and temporary. Layout changes capture the first visible
source block and restore its viewport position after reflow where possible, rather
than persisting a second text offset or editing manuscript content.

Paragraph ellipsis buttons, pointer context menus and keyboard context-menu
shortcuts share the same action builder. A valid single-paragraph selection
offers a small toolbar. Marker and claim actions delegate to the established
handlers, including their explicit save, capability and retention checks; no
parallel write API is introduced. Values reuse the paragraph's measured markup
